newsitem.title: USA: Ukraine seeks U.S. help in battling corruption.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine seeks U.S. help in battling corruption.

text.p: A senior Ukrainian official, ahead of a U.S. visit by President Leonid Kuchma, acknowledged on Monday that his country has serious corruption problems and said it is seeking help to deal with it, including from the Central Intelligence Agency.

"Corruption does exist in Ukraine ... We are aware that corruption is the main reason for the stopping of reforms in Ukraine," Volodymyr Horbulin told a small breakfast meeting at the Ukrainian ambassador's residence.
"We would be very grateful for any assistance ... I want to make clear we're not going to hide anything... Please help us to get rid of every evil," he said through an interpreter.
He stressed that Ukraine had been a totalitarian system for 70 years before gaining independence five years ago and cited this as a major reason for the problem.

Horbulin, secretary of Ukraine's national security and defense council, was in Washington for talks with Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and other officials ahead of Kuchma's visit on Thursday and Friday.
The "toughest questions" to be confronted during the visit concern Ukraine's economy, he said.
He acknowledged Ukraine's economy was not reformed enough to qualify now for NATO membership but said he hoped it could qualify sooner than the 2010 date suggested by some experts.

Horbulin said he discussed the corruption issue previously with former CIA Director John Deutch and sought help from the agency in combatting the problem, such as alerting Kiev to any corruption behind any business transactions.

"They promised us, but not a single fact was ever mentioned to the Ukrainian side by the CIA," he said. He planned to raise the issue of U.S. assistance again during this week's talks in Washington, he said.

The Washington Post reported on Monday that congressional opposition to American aid to Ukraine was stiffening because of mounting reports of lawless practices afflicting U.S. business in that country. Ukraine is a major aid recipient.

The newspaper cited legislation approved last week by a key House of Representatives committee that would permit the president to cut off foreign assistance for Kiev unless it cracks down on official and unofficial corruption highlighted at several hearings in the past month.
The full House may vote on the measure on Wednesday, the day Kuchma is due to arrive in the U.S. capital after completing a visit to Moscow.
Anton Buteiko, Ukraine's first deputy foreign affairs minister, said he found it suspicious that the Post's story appeared at the same time as Kuchma's planned visits to Washington and to Moscow.
He said some people, whom he did not name, oppose Ukraine establishing good relations with the United States and Russia.

"Therefore I'm sure it is not a coincidence that that issue of corruption suddenly was brought up on the eve of the two visits" and when Ukraine is on the verge of privatizing large industries, Buteiko said.
He said more than 200 American firms are working on investments in Ukraine and some have raised legitimate complaints that the government is trying to remedy.
Despite contrary reports, Russia and Ukraine have not yet resolved the fate of 42-43 strategic nuclear bombers that Kiev controls but wants to be rid of, Horbulin said.

Ukraine gave the last of its nuclear weapons to Russia last year and has no need for the bombers but Russia has now refused to take the bombers even at the "very low price" it first offered Kiev, Horbulin said, adding: "If we can't give them to Russia, then we should destroy them."

He said he did not believe Russia and Belarus would ever unite and argued strongly for the United States and other countries to "do everything to preserve independence for Belarus," despite its turn toward totalitarianism.
